constitutive_assumptions: Grasped objects are simplified to axis-symmetric geometry around the longitudinal axis for analytical contact modeling
Coulomb kinetic friction with a constant kinetic friction coefficient between the finger surface and the conical contact surface during insertion and removal
Super-elastic material behavior of the internal nitinol backbone strip
Linear relationship between applied load on the FlexiForce sensor and operational amplifier output voltage
control_variables: Cone insertion and retraction rate (1 mm/s)
Finger geometry (6.45 cm length, 120-degree radial spacing, 20-degree vertical offset, 30-degree fingertip pad offset)
Control loop interrupt frequency (10 kHz on Arduino Mega 2560)
PID controller parameters (Kp = 4000, KI = 0, KD = 125, error shut-off tolerance = 0.025 N)
Postharvest storage environment (vented clamshell containers with 20 berries per clamshell at 2 degrees Celsius for 21 days)
dependent_variables: Applied fingertip contact force (measured by ATI force sensor and Vernier sensor)
Fingertip force tracking error and handling standard deviation
Harvesting reliability percentage (successful harvests divided by total attempts)
Red drupelet reversion (RDR) percentage after postharvest cold storage

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The tendon-driven soft robotic gripper with closed-loop contact force control applied forces from 0.50 N to 1.45 N with a mean tracking error of 0.046 N and a standard deviation of 0.027 N, achieving a 26-fold reduction in handling force variability compared to manual picking.

In commercial field harvesting trials on blackberries, higher contact force increased harvesting reliability but also elevated red drupelet reversion; a 0.78 N setpoint resulted in 95.24% reliability and 16% RDR, whereas a 0.59 N setpoint yielded 0% RDR but lower reliability (81.08%).

Empirical contact force characterization using cone push-pull force summation eliminated the unknown friction coefficient to construct a 3D relationship between tendon displacement (5-9 mm), target diameter (0-47 mm), and normal contact force, peaking at 4.92 N.

Manual force tracking across 1,440 hand-picked blackberries revealed that thumb and middle fingers contribute the primary contact forces (0.782 N and 0.397 N), while the ring finger force is negligible.
Incorporating a 0.3 mm super-elastic nitinol backbone strip into molded silicone fingers increased transverse bending stiffness by 134 times while maintaining compliance in the flexure direction.

experimental_setup: Manual harvesting force measurement apparatus equipped with FlexiForce A301 piezoresistive sensors mounted to fingers of an experienced harvester connected to a portable water-resistant processing case
Benchtop force control accuracy station comparing gripper fingertip forces against a rigid 6-axis ATI force sensor aligned parallel to the curved finger pad on a linear table

Empirical contact force characterization testbed comprising a 3D-printed cone (15-degree draft angle) driven at 1 mm/s by an SFU1605 ball screw and NEMA 23 stepper motor with a Vernier Go Direct force sensor
Grasping versatility testing on 12 objects of daily living with varied geometry, stiffness, and mass
Field harvesting trial on 240 Sweet-Ark Caddo blackberries at a commercial farm comparing three robot force setpoints against manual harvesting, evaluated after 21 days at 2 degrees Celsius
future_work: System-level integration of the soft gripper with a robotic arm and mobile robot chassis using SLAM and computer vision for autonomous localization and harvesting
Tuning PID control gains and optimizing pre-grasp home finger positions to decrease harvest cycle time
Incorporating fruit diameter into the control and positioning strategy to reduce actuation time
Estimating fingertip forces indirectly by mapping tendon tension in joint space to task space to eliminate rigid fingertip sensor supports
Optimizing fingertip geometry to enhance dexterity and grasping performance
Investigating gripper robustness and disturbance response against plant canes and foliage
Identifying an optimal contact force setpoint that balances harvest reliability and minimum red drupelet reversion
independent_variables: Target fingertip contact force setpoints (0.50 N to 1.45 N in benchtop testing; 0.59 N, 0.69 N, and 0.78 N in field harvesting tests)
Tendon retraction displacement (5 mm to 9 mm in 0.5 mm steps)
Grasped object diameter (0 mm to 47 mm across conical and ADL objects)
Object physical characteristics (geometry, stiffness, surface compliance across 12 test items)
Harvesting method (soft robotic gripper vs. manual hand harvesting)
limitations_inferred: Field harvesting evaluations were restricted to a single blackberry cultivar (Sweet-Ark Caddo) at a single location, leaving performance on other cultivars with differing detachment forces unverified
Contact force characterization employed a rigid 3D-printed cone, which does not simulate the local contact deformation and compliance of soft aggregate berries
Manual positioning of the gripper during field trials bypassed the dynamics, inaccuracies, and vibrations of an autonomous manipulator arm
Analytical contact formulation assumes idealized Coulomb friction, which may not capture adhesive or viscoelastic characteristics of biological produce
limitations_stated_by_authors: Gripper placement was executed manually rather than autonomously due to the difficulty of cane and berry localization
Robotic harvest cycle time (~4.8 s per berry) was approximately 3.4 times slower than hand harvesting (1.4 s per berry) due to slow actuator response
Control feedback is restricted solely to fingertip contact force, omitting berry diameter and task-space geometry
Rigid 3D-printed cylindrical PLA force sensor backing supports on the fingertips present a risk of fruit surface bruising
Objects with diameters below 10 mm cannot be sufficiently grasped by the gripper geometry
Silicone-only fingers have low transverse stiffness and are susceptible to disturbances from cane collisions without the nitinol strip
main_results: The closed-loop force-controlled gripper achieved an average contact force error of 0.046 N across setpoints from 0.50 N to 1.45 N, and reduced force standard deviation to 0.027 N compared to 0.702 N for human pickers

In field trials, the gripper at 0.78 N contact force achieved 95.24% harvesting reliability with 16% RDR at ~4.8 s per berry, outperforming manual harvest RDR (33.33%) while maintaining high reliability
Lower contact force (0.59 N) eliminated RDR entirely (0%) but decreased harvesting reliability to 81.08% and increased harvesting time to ~8.1 s per berry
Normal fingertip contact force was characterized up to 4.92 N at 9 mm tendon retraction and 47 mm diameter, demonstrating grasping capacity across common blackberry sizes (>20 mm)
Versatility testing confirmed stable grasping of diverse ADL objects including delicate produce, soft fabrics, rigid cans, and jars
modeling_methods: 2D static equilibrium force balance on a conical geometry during push and pull phases to cancel kinetic friction and isolate the normal fingertip contact force
Empirical curve fitting and 3D surface mesh generation in MATLAB to model normal contact force as a function of tendon displacement and object diameter
performance_metrics: Contact force standard deviation across trials (N)
Red drupelet reversion (RDR) incidence percentage (%) after 21-day cold storage
possible_gap_implications: The noticeable cycle time deficit compared to manual picking (~4.8 s vs. 1.4 s) indicates a need for faster tendon drive mechanisms and predictive trajectory planning before soft robotic harvesters become commercially viable

The trade-off between picking reliability and RDR suggests that fixed-force setpoints may be suboptimal, pointing toward multi-phase or variable-stiffness grasping where higher force is applied during detachment and reduced during holding
Reliance on rigid sensor backing discs highlights the gap in compliant, non-damaging tactile sensing integration for delicate agricultural soft robotics
paper.research_objective: To design, fabricate, and experimentally evaluate a tendon-driven soft robotic gripper with closed-loop contact force control capable of harvesting delicate fresh-market blackberries gently and reliably to minimize red drupelet reversion (RDR).
paper.research_problem: Fresh-market blackberry harvesting is an expensive, labor-intensive process (accounting for up to 50% of production person-hours) where manual handling variability causes significant crop loss from red drupelet reversion (RDR, up to 85%), while conventional automated harvesting methods damage the delicate berry surface.
stiffness_mechanism: inherent passive compliance of silicone material
paper.title: Tendon-Driven Soft Robotic Gripper for Blackberry Harvesting
